source_text: Dixi, quod erat primum, scientiam boni non esse uirtutem, deinde, quid sit uirtus et in quo sit: sequitur ut id quoque ipsum, quid sit bonum et malum, nescisse philosophos breuiter ostendam, quia paene declaratum est in libro tertio, cum de summo bono disputarem. qui autem quid esset summum nescierunt, et in ceteris bonis malisue, quae summa non sunt, errauerint necesse est: quae non potest uero iudicio examinare qui fontem ipsum non tenet unde illa descendunt. fons autem bonorum deus est, malorum uero ille scilicet diuini nominis semper inimicus, de quo saepe diximus: ab his duobus principiis bona malaque oriuntur. quae ueniunt a deo, hanc habent rationem, ut inmortalitatem parent, quod est summum bonum: quae autem ab illo altero, id habent officium, ut a caelestibus auocatum terrenisque demersum ad poenam interficiant sempiternam, quod est summum malum. num igitur dubium est quin illi omnes quid esset bonum et malum ignoraueriut, qui nec deum nec aduersarium dei scierunt? itaque finem bonorum ad corpus et ad hanc uitam breuem retulerunt, quam scilicet solui et occidere necesse est, non sunt progressi ulterius, sed omnia eorum praecepta et omnia quae inducunt bona, terrae inhaerent et humi iacent, quoniam simul cum corpore, quod est terra, moriuntur. pertinent enim non ad uitam homini conparandam, sed ad quaerendas uel augendas opes honores gloriam potentiam: quae sunt uniuersa mortalia, tam scilicet quam ille qui ut ea sibi contingerent laborauit. hinc est illud: uirtus, quaerendae finem rei scire modumque. praecipiunt enim quibus modis et quibus artibus res familiaris quaerenda sit, quia uident male quaeri solere. sed huiusmodi uirtus non est proposita sapienti: nec enim uirtus est opes quaerere, quarum neque inuentio neque possessio in nostra potestate est. itaque et quaesitu et obtentu faciliores sunt malis quam bonis. non potest ergo uirtus esse in iis rebus quaerendis in quarum contemptu uis ac ratio uirtutis apparet, nec ad ea ipsa transfugiet quae magno et excelso animo calcare ac proterere gestit, neque fas est animam caelestibus intentam bonis, ut haec fragilia sibi conparet, ab inmortalibus suis opibus auocari, sed potissimum in iis rebus conparandis uirtutis ratio consistit quas nobis nec homo ullus nec mors ipsa possit auferre.
pass_a_gloss: I said what was first, that knowledge of good is not virtue, then what virtue is and in what it is: it follows that I must also briefly show that philosophers were ignorant of what good and evil are, because it was almost declared in the third book, when I was disputing about the highest good: those who were ignorant of what the highest good is, and erred in other goods and evils, which are not the highest, it is necessary: which cannot truly be examined by judgment, who does not hold the source itself from which those things come. But the source of goods is God, of evils truly that one, always enemy of the divine name, about whom we have often spoken: from these two principles goods and evils arise. Which come from God, have this reason, that they bring immortality, which is the highest good: which however from that other, have this duty, that they kill and destroy, having been called away from heavenly things and immersed in earthly things, to eternal punishment, which is the highest evil. Is it therefore doubtful that all those were ignorant of what good and evil are, who knew neither God nor the adversary of God? And so they referred the end of goods to the body and to this brief life, which certainly must be dissolved and killed, they did not progress further, but all their precepts and all the goods they introduce, cling to the earth and lie on the ground, because they die together with the body, which is earth. For they pertain not to the life of man to be compared, but to seeking or increasing wealth, honors, glory, power: which are all mortal, as certainly as he who labored that these things might happen to him. From this is that saying: virtue, to know the end of a thing and its measure. For they teach by what means and arts family wealth is to be sought, because they see it is usually sought badly. But such virtue is not proposed to the wise: for virtue is not to seek wealth, the discovery or possession of which is not in our power. And so both the seeking and the obtaining are easier for evils than for goods. Therefore virtue cannot be in those things that are sought, in whose contempt the power and reason of virtue appear, nor will it flee to those things themselves which it strives to trample and despise with a great and lofty mind, nor is it right that the soul, intent on heavenly goods, should be called away from its immortal goods to compare these fragile things to itself, but rather the reason of virtue consists in those things that are to be compared, which no man nor death itself can take away from us.
pass_b_english: First I argued that knowing what is good is not the same as virtue; then I defined virtue and showed where it resides. It follows that I must now briefly demonstrate that the philosophers were ignorant of what good and evil truly are, since this was nearly proven in the third book when I discussed the highest good. Those who did not know the highest good necessarily erred concerning all other goods and evils, which are not the highest; no one can rightly judge these things who does not grasp the very source from which they flow. The source of all good is God; the source of evil is the one who is the constant enemy of the divine name, whom I have often mentioned. From these two principles all good and evil originate. Whatever comes from God has this purpose: it brings immortality, which is the highest good. Whatever comes from that other source has this function: it kills and destroys those who have been drawn away from heavenly things and plunged into earthly things, consigning them to eternal punishment, which is the highest evil. Is it doubtful, then, that all those philosophers were ignorant of good and evil, since they knew neither God nor God's adversary? Consequently they limited the end of all goods to the body and to this brief life, which must inevitably dissolve and die; they advanced no further. All their precepts and all the goods they propose cling to the earth and lie in the dust, because they perish together with the body, which is earth. These things do not pertain to the true life of man, but to the pursuit or increase of wealth, honors, glory, and power — all of which are mortal, just like the person who toiled to obtain them. Hence the saying: virtue consists in knowing the end and measure of a thing. For they teach the means and arts by which family wealth is to be sought, because they see it is usually sought badly. But such virtue is not set before the wise; virtue is not the quest for wealth, whose discovery and possession are not in our power. Thus both the seeking and the obtaining of wealth are easier for the wicked than for the good. Therefore virtue cannot reside in those things which are sought, since it is in despising them that virtue's power and reason appear; nor will virtue turn to those very things which a great and lofty soul strives to trample and spurn. Nor is it right that a soul intent on heavenly goods should be diverted from its immortal possessions to acquire these fragile things. Rather, the reason of virtue consists in securing those goods which neither any human being nor death itself can take from us.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A preserves the syntax and nuances of the original, and Pass B provides a fluent, accurate rendering. All clauses, including the distinction between the two principles and the definition of virtue, are accounted for.
